title: Plan the eval gate for a support agent before launch: test set, graders, pass bar and CI step
scenario: An online shop will launch a support agent in two weeks. The team drafted its launch gate: a test set, a model judge, a release check, an attack run and a CI schedule. Five parts of the draft look weak. You review the draft in the exhibit.
exhibit:
(made-up example data)

BRIEF:
  An online shop launches a support agent in 2 weeks.
  Tools: lookup_order, issue_refund (limit $100), escalate_to_human.
  The team plans a launch gate that runs in CI: tasks, graders and a pass bar.

TEST SET (draft):
  40 tasks, taken from last quarter's support tickets.
  Each ticket was tidied by hand before it became a task:
  one complete, polite sentence, one question, no typos.

JUDGE (draft), for the check "the explanation was clear and correct":
  Experts labelled 100 agent answers: 40 fail, 60 pass.
  The team edited the judge prompt on all 100 answers until it matched the experts on 93 of them.
    failures found:  36 of 40   (TPR 90%)
    passes found:    57 of 60   (TNR 95%)
  team note: "Both rates are above 90%. The judge is ready."

RELEASE CHECK (draft):
  The regression suite: the 40 tasks, 1 trial each, run once before each release.
  Release 1 passed 40 of 40.
  Two days after launch, customers report answers that are sometimes garbled.
  The team re-runs the suite on the live system: 40 of 40 again.

ATTACKS (draft):
  120 attack runs against the full pipeline, every layer on: 4 succeeded.
  Layers: input screen, system prompt rules, tool guardrail on issue_refund, output filter.
  The lead asks: "Which layer is doing the work?"

CI (draft):
  File: .github/workflows/evals-nightly.yml
  Trigger: schedule, cron "0 3 * * *" (full suite and attack set every night)
  Job: timeout-minutes: 20
  The file exists only on the branch feature/eval-gate.
  The repository has commits every day.
  After 3 nights, the Actions tab shows no run of this workflow.

questions.prompt: All 40 tasks are tidy, single-question sentences. What should the team add to the test set?

options.text: Forty more tidy tickets in the same style, so the set grows to 80 tasks and each change shows a clearer effect.
options.explanation: More of the same shape adds volume, not coverage. The OpenAI docs warn about datasets that don't faithfully reproduce production traffic patterns.

options.text: Only attack prompts such as "ignore your rules", because normal requests are already covered by the 40 tickets.
options.explanation: The OpenAI docs say test data should include typical cases, edge cases and adversarial cases. Tidied tickets are not typical traffic, and attacks alone drop the typical cases.

options.text: Tasks with typos, two questions in one message, and very short requests such as the single word "returns".
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's evaluation guide lists multiple intents in one request, typos and misspellings, and short requests with minimal context (its example is "returns") as cases to test.

options.text: Nothing. The tickets are real customer data, so the set already matches what users send to the agent.
options.explanation: The tickets were tidied by hand, so they no longer look like real messages. The OpenAI docs name this as biased design: a dataset that does not reproduce production traffic.

questions.prompt: The team says both rates are above 90%, so the judge is ready. What is missing?

options.text: A held-out test set. Keep about 40% of the labels out of tuning, then run the judge on them once at the end.
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI Cookbook splits expert labels about 20% train, 40% validation and 40% test. The test set is held out and run one time, to confirm you haven't overfit.

options.text: Nothing is missing. A TPR of 90% and a TNR of 95% on expert labels is exactly what the Cookbook asks for.
options.explanation: The Cookbook sets no number; it asks for high TPR and TNR on a held-out test set. These rates come from the same 100 answers used for tuning, which can hide overfitting.

options.text: More tuning. Edit the prompt again on the same 100 answers until both rates reach 100%, then ship it.
options.explanation: More tuning on the same answers makes the overfitting worse. The Cookbook keeps a test set that is not used for tuning.

options.text: One accuracy number. Report 93 of 100 to the gate, because a single figure is easier to use than two.
options.explanation: The Cookbook uses TPR and TNR because plain accuracy can hide a judge that never finds a failure. The two rates are the right numbers; the missing part is a held-out test.

questions.prompt: The suite passes 40 of 40 twice, but customers report garbled answers. What does Anthropic's postmortem suggest for the gate?

options.text: Trust the suite. Two clean runs of 40 of 40 show the reports come from a few users, so keep the gate as it is.
options.explanation: Anthropic's postmortem says its own evals simply didn't capture the degradation users were reporting. A green suite is not proof.

options.text: Run the same release check three times before every release, so a bad release has more chances to be caught.
options.explanation: The same tasks, run only before release, would still miss it. Anthropic's fix was more sensitive evals, run on production systems.

options.text: Drop the suite and rely on customer reports alone, because the evals missed the problem and users saw it first.
options.explanation: Anthropic kept its evals and made them better. Reports come after the damage; evals are the early check.

options.text: Add tasks that tell a working system from a broken one, and run the suite continuously on the live system.
options.explanation: Right. The Anthropic postmortem says the team's evals didn't capture the degradation users reported. The fixes: evals that more reliably differentiate working from broken implementations, and running them continuously on true production systems.

questions.prompt: All four layers were on in the 120 attack runs. What should the team run next to see which layer stops which attacks?

options.text: The 120 attacks once with all four layers off, so the raw model result shows which layer matters most.
options.explanation: That shows only the model alone. It does not show what each single layer adds when the others are on.

options.text: The same 120 attacks again with one layer off at a time, then compare which attacks get through.
options.explanation: Right. This is our own habit from the lesson, not a vendor rule: keep the full-pipeline run, then switch off single layers to learn which layer caught each attack.

options.text: Each layer alone, outside the pipeline, because layers are the parts that the team can change one by one.
options.explanation: Users reach the whole pipeline, so the full run stays. Layers alone also miss how they work together.

options.text: The same 120 attacks ten times each with every layer on, because a larger sample shows which layer matters.
options.explanation: More runs help with varying outputs, but the setup is the same. With every layer on, a run can't show which layer did the work.

questions.prompt: The nightly workflow never runs. What is the cause, and what is the fix?

options.text: A schedule runs only while a pull request is open. Add a pull_request trigger and open a draft PR.
options.explanation: A schedule trigger does not depend on open pull requests. The docs name the default branch as the limit.

options.text: The run is cancelled for taking too long. Raise timeout-minutes from 20 to 60.
options.explanation: A cancelled run would still appear in the Actions tab. Here no run appears at all.

options.text: GitHub runs scheduled workflows only from the default branch. Merge the workflow file into it.
options.explanation: Right. The Claude Code docs say GitHub runs scheduled workflows only from the default branch. A file that lives only on feature/eval-gate never fires.

options.text: GitHub disables schedules after 60 days without activity. Turn the schedule back on in the Actions tab.
options.explanation: The docs say this applies to public repositories after 60 days without repository activity. This repository has commits every day.
